Mayor Unveils $180 Million Flood-Resilience Plan After Back-to-Back Storms

By Staff Reporter  
March 9, 2026

RIVERTON — After two major storms in less than three months inundated neighborhoods, forced road closures, and left thousands without power, Mayor Elena Park on Monday announced a $180 million flood-resilience initiative aimed at reducing damage in the city’s most vulnerable areas.

The multi-year plan, branded “Riverton Ready,” combines traditional drainage upgrades with green infrastructure projects such as rain gardens and permeable pavement. City officials said the first phase will prioritize the low-lying Eastbank and Harborview districts, where residents have reported repeated basement flooding and stormwater backups.

“We can’t keep treating these storms as one-off events,” Park said during a morning press conference outside City Hall, where public works crews were still clearing debris from last week’s downpour. “Riverton has to be built for the climate we’re living in now—more intense rainfall, higher tides, and more frequent flooding.”

According to the city’s Office of Emergency Management, the Feb. 22 storm dropped 4.7 inches of rain in 24 hours, followed by a March 3 system that brought another 3.9 inches alongside strong winds. Officials said the two events caused an estimated $35 million in public infrastructure damage and prompted more than 1,200 calls to the city’s non-emergency line, many related to flooded streets and downed trees.

What the plan includes

The package, which will go to the City Council for an initial vote next week, allocates:

- $72 million for enlarging stormwater pipes and replacing undersized culverts at 18 identified choke points  
- $41 million for installing pump stations and backflow preventers near the waterfront  
- $28 million for green infrastructure, including curbside bioswales, expanded tree canopy, and permeable alleys  
- $22 million for elevating critical road segments used by ambulances and buses  
- $17 million for home protection grants, including subsidized sump pumps and flood vents for qualifying households

Public Works Director Malcolm Reyes said engineering surveys conducted over the past year found “capacity issues that were manageable a decade ago” but are now failing during high-intensity rainfall. “We have pipes designed for a different era,” Reyes said. “This is about bringing the system up to what the city is experiencing today.”

Funding and timeline

City budget officials said the proposal relies on a mix of municipal bonds, state resilience grants, and federal disaster-mitigation funds. Finance Committee Chair Dana Whitaker cautioned that the plan’s bond component could face scrutiny amid rising borrowing costs.

“We agree on the need,” Whitaker said in an interview. “The question is sequencing—what we can do immediately, what we can phase in, and how we avoid placing the burden on ratepayers.”

If approved, construction on the first set of drainage upgrades could begin by late summer, with green infrastructure pilots starting as early as May. The city expects the full program to run five to seven years.

Residents weigh urgency against disruption

In Eastbank, where floodwaters spilled over Maple Street during the March 3 storm, some residents welcomed the announcement but expressed frustration at the pace of previous repairs.

“We’ve been filing reports for years,” said Jasmine Lee, who lives in a duplex near the canal. “I’m glad it’s finally being taken seriously, but we need action before the next storm season.”

Others said they worry about the disruption that prolonged street work could bring. “We want solutions, but our block can’t be torn up for months without a plan for parking and access,” said Carlos Mendes, owner of a small grocery on 8th Avenue.

Environmental groups largely praised the inclusion of green infrastructure, arguing it can complement large-scale pipe replacements by absorbing runoff before it reaches the sewer system.

“Concrete alone won’t solve this,” said Priya Nand, director of the Riverton Watershed Alliance. “Trees, wetlands restoration, and permeable surfaces are key to keeping water out of basements and pollutants out of the river.”

Next steps

The City Council is scheduled to hold a public hearing Thursday evening, with a committee vote expected next week. Park’s office said an interactive project map and a sign-up portal for home protection grants will go live within two weeks.

For residents like Lee, the test will be whether the promises translate into fewer sandbags and sleepless nights.

“Every time the forecast says heavy rain, we’re on edge,” she said. “If this means we can finally breathe, then it can’t come soon enough.”
